title: A Thousand Companies a Year and a China Branch: YC, Silicon Valley's Biggest Startup Incubator, on How Fast It Wants to Go
excerpt: Sam Altman, Y Combinator's new head, has a long list of things he wants to do
body:
Sam Altman, Y Combinator's new head, has a long list of things he wants to do

"Grow fast, or die slowly."

For the past decade, this line about startups from Paul Graham, founder of the Silicon Valley tech incubator YC (Y Combinator), has driven the more than 900 startups YC has incubated.

Now YC itself is the one chasing fast growth. Over the past year, each batch it trains has grown from 58 companies to 120. The combined market value of the startups it funds has jumped from US$20 billion to US$50 billion.

Sam Altman, the man who led that growth, turned 30 this month. Interviewed by QDaily in Shenzhen last Friday, he laid out an even bigger to-do list:

- Consider opening a YC branch in China;
- Consider providing venture capital to more mature startups;
- Next year, extend YC's incubation to startups at a later stage;
- Five years from now, fund a thousand startups a year — as many as in the past 10 years combined.

Before 2014, only a handful of people who knew YC very well knew who Altman was. To outsiders, YC was essentially Graham's personal project.

Graham, who built the world's first commercial web software and sold his company for nearly US$50 million, is perhaps the most influential writer among programmers. Over the past dozen or so years, the essays on his personal website, [paulgraham.com](http://paulgraham.com/), have circulated widely, and his 2004 collection *Hackers & Painters* overturned many people's ideas about computer science.

In 2005, Graham noticed that the cost of starting an internet company had fallen sharply. With a few friends, he founded YC to give young founders money and basic support. As the first tech startup incubator, YC works more like a school.

Mentors, including Graham, Peter Thiel and Gmail's creator Paul Buchheit, talk often with the young founders and help them solve the problems they hit while building a company. Every week the participants also eat dinner together and hear well-known entrepreneurs such as Mark Zuckerberg and Marc Andreessen talk about their own experiences.

After ten years, the startups YC has incubated form a distinct group in Silicon Valley, known as YC startups or YC companies. The most successful of them, Airbnb and Dropbox, are each valued at more than US$10 billion.

Altman himself was in YC's very first batch. He was 20, and had just dropped out of college to build a mobile app called Loopt, which let friends share their current locations. Loopt was eventually sold, but along the way Altman became a part-time partner at YC, investing in YC startups and advising them.

In February 2014, Graham announced that Altman would take over as president and run YC from then on, saying YC needed to grow faster and Altman was the best person for the job. Graham then stepped back from day-to-day management and handed most of his YC shares to Altman and the other YC partners.

Over the following year, we saw what Altman changed. The startup course, once taught in person inside YC with no journalists or other outsiders allowed in, became a 17-episode online course, [*How To Start A Startup*](http://startupclass.samaltman.com/), free to anyone in the world.

YC, which had focused on software startups, also spread into more fields over the past year — almost any field. At this March's Demo Day for investors and the media, the YC projects on show included a prison management platform, an anti-Ebola drug and a low-orbit rocket. Before that, YC had even taken in Helion Energy, a nuclear fusion startup.

YC's two leaders clearly have different styles. Graham teaches like a patient professor, leading his audience step by step. Altman talks fast and answers briefly, whether he is sharing startup lessons in the video course or answering our questions.

Asked whether he misses being a founder, Altman said his work at YC "still makes me feel like I'm running a startup. YC is a bit different from other investment firms, and I think that's a good thing." [Asked the same question two years ago](http://www.inc.com/magazine/201309/issie-lapowsky/how-paul-graham-became-successful.html), Graham answered: "I never want to do that again. Being an investor is so much easier than starting a company."

This trip to Shenzhen is Altman's second visit to China since joining YC. In the interview, he listed a rather large to-do list for us:

- Assess whether to open a YC branch in China;
- Consider providing venture capital to mature startups;
- Next year, extend YC's incubation to startups at a later stage;
- Five years from now, fund a thousand startups a year — as many as in the past 10 years combined.

Under Altman, YC looks a little less like a tutoring class for founders and more like an ambitious investment firm. Keeping the startups closely connected at this scale will be a challenge, and a bigger scale often also means a lower bar to entry and more standardized training.

But perhaps, as YC's own creed puts it, a YC that has itself gone into startup mode will either grow fast or die slowly. Those are the only two choices.

More detail is in the full interview below (the order has been rearranged).

## What does YC want to do in China? "The first thing is to figure out: should we open a YC China?"

**QDaily: Is this your first time in China?**

Altman: No, it's my third. I came once in 2009 and once in 2014. I was already at YC then. I think China is the hottest place for entrepreneurs.

Also, I don't think there will be just one "new Silicon Valley"; there will be many new Silicon Valleys around the world. But if you had to pick just one, it would basically be Beijing.

**QDaily: In your advice to startups, you say founders should focus on two or three things a day and turn themselves into an execution machine. What are your goals today?**

Altman: I'm traveling, so it's mostly meeting reporters, visiting some factories, and a meeting in Hong Kong this afternoon.

But the first item on my list is to figure out: should we open a YC China? And if we do, how?

**QDaily: Is there a plan yet?**

Altman: Not yet, we're still thinking about it. I'll make a decision after talking it over with the other partners. We're still working out exactly what to do about mentors and infrastructure.

**QDaily: Why China?**

Altman: There's no better place in the world for tech startups. Most of the tech companies worth more than US$10 billion that were founded in the past decade came from either the United States or China. We're already in the United States, so China is the right place.

**QDaily: You must have heard a lot over the past few days, from startups and incubator people, about government support for entrepreneurship. What do you think of the government pushing startups?**

Altman: I did hear quite a lot. But we always say we want more good startups, not more startups. My worry is that if you encourage entrepreneurship, you can always attract more startups. The important question is whether that produces good startups. That's the real question.

**QDaily: Yesterday you said there's an incubator bubble. When did you realize that?**

Altman: On this trip to China.

Compared with when I came last year, the stock market is 2.5 times higher. And on this trip I've also seen hundreds of incubators.

**QDaily: What does the worst kind of incubator look like to you?**

Altman: We've never liked incubators where all the founders work in one space, and that's what most incubators do. It's a really bad choice.

Shared office space can be a good business; WeWork is now valued at US$5 billion. But it's not a good environment for startups.

The most obvious problem is the distraction of working together. Another very bad problem is that the best startup ideas always sound a bit crazy. If a team works on its own, it's a bit like a secret mission, a secret you don't share with anyone. But in a shared space, when you mention your crazy idea in casual chat, you get negative feedback.

## What has changed at YC? "My batch had only 8 companies, and the latest batch has 120"

**QDaily: You joined YC's first batch as a founder in 2005. Ten years on, what has changed?**

Altman: My batch had only 8 companies, and the latest one has 120. That's 15 times as many.

My batch had no community; we were the first batch. Now there's a tightly connected community, and the companies help each other. That opens up a huge number of possibilities.

We've invested in more than 900 startups, and when they join they agree to one thing: you have to help other YC startups. On your first day at YC, every YC startup is your friend.

Take Stripe, the payments company. Its first 20 customers were almost all YC startups. Now, when a new YC company needs to sort out payments, Stripe helps.

**QDaily: It's been more than a year since Graham handed you the top job. What have you done in that time?**

Altman: The number of startups in each batch has more than doubled. When I took over, all YC companies together were worth about US$20 billion. Now it's US$50 billion.

When I took over, we had 58 companies per batch; now we have 120.

When I took over, we mainly invested in software companies, plus a few hardware companies. Now we cover rocket companies, biotech companies, nuclear energy companies... everything.

Another thing: we've launched a set of services to help startups hire and raise money better, rather than just teaching more classes.

**QDaily: I watched your startup course and it's excellent. But why did it only go online last year? Whose idea was it?**

Altman: Mine. One problem YC has to solve is that we need to work very closely with the startups we incubate. But now 15,000 startups apply to YC every year, and we can't take more than 14,700 of them. If we can help more people, that's obviously a good thing.

So we decided to put what we teach at YC online and let other startups watch it for free. The feedback was very good. Thousands of startups applied to YC after watching the videos.

We plan to translate the whole course into Chinese, a complete translation. There are already volunteer translations online.

**QDaily: YC's first lesson is about how hard starting a company is and how painful a founder's life will be. Why design it that way?**

Altman: I really believe the truth is the best advertising. We want to warn people what this is actually like. In the United States, starting a company is something of a fashion. Many people want to do it because they think it will raise their social status and make them look cool.

But in fact, it's very, very hard. We want people to know that.

## How does YC work? "A tech startup isn't just about technology; it's more about the company"

**QDaily: There are now 120 companies in a YC batch, so there must be more than 200 founders. How do you organize YC's traditional weekly dinners and training?**

Altman: There are now more than 300 founders in a batch. We split them into four groups, and each startup joins one. The people in your group are the ones you deal with most, and you get to know each other very well. You can see it in this photo:

![Founders at a YC batch dinner](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160604221829S09lu8Mapi4emndX.jpg-w600)

It's like a giant college dining hall.

**QDaily: When did you start splitting into groups? Do you group by type of company?**

Altman: About two years ago, when there were already too many people for anyone to know everyone.

The groups are completely random. We once tried putting companies of the same type in one group, but then decided it was better for different types of companies to connect with each other. The most important thing isn't software startups versus non-software startups; it's connecting everyone who is starting a company.

**QDaily: What can a nuclear energy company learn from other companies?**

Altman: A startup isn't just about technology; it's more about the company. You can learn a lot: how to recruit executives, how to run a company, how to talk to investors, whether to hold an all-hands meeting every week, how to fire people, how to do sales and marketing well. Every company has to deal with many of these things.

Of course, they still have to make fusion power work on their own, and that's very hard.

**QDaily: Is there any limit to the kinds of startups YC will take?**

Altman: We're willing to fund any startup we think could become a billion-dollar business. So whatever the industry, if we think it could become a billion-dollar business, we'll get involved.

**QDaily: What does the perfect startup mentor look like to you?**

Altman: Someone who has started a company and run one.

It's very, very hard to understand what a founder is going through unless you've started a company yourself. Executives at big companies just don't have that experience.

YC has 20 mentors. All of them are partners, and only partners are mentors. Other well-known speakers, like Zuckerberg, are just guests. Peter Thiel used to be a guest speaker too, and later he joined us.

**QDaily: Last year you changed YC's investment to US$120,000 for 7% of the equity. Why is that the right number?**

Altman: It came out of a lot of experiments. At first it was US$20,000 for 5%, then it became US$170,000, then US$100,000, then US$80,000, and finally we settled on US$120,000.

Too much money is bad: it makes a startup lose focus, and you want to do too many things. If there's little money, you can only focus on one project, and you have to make it succeed.

But too little money is also bad, because it runs out too soon. We try to find the perfect balance. The cost of living in the San Francisco Bay Area has gone up a lot, so we added some on top of US$80,000.

**QDaily: At many venture capital firms, analysts do the homework that helps investors decide whether to back a company. What about YC?**

Altman: YC doesn't do that. Every partner has to do the basic homework themselves. For example, I did the research on that nuclear energy project myself.

Very occasionally, we invest in projects whose workings we don't fully understand, but only if we can find someone who does.

## How does YC pick companies? "Good ideas usually sound pretty good, but at the time they also seem to have some problems"

**QDaily: You often say that when you look at a founding team, what matters most is the people and the idea. But how do you judge an idea? Back then, did you really think a platform for watching other people play games could become a billion-dollar business?**

Altman: No, I wouldn't have thought so at the time. Here's the thing about ideas: you have to take some risk. Good ideas usually sound pretty good, but at the time they also seem to have some problems.

If an idea is obviously good, a great many people are already working on it. When Twitch started, it wasn't quite what it is today. Justin Kan's original plan was to wear a camera on his head so you could watch his life 24x7. Building on that, they eventually found that what people watched most was him playing games. And out of that, Twitch was born.

So I don't think we realized back then that it was a good idea. In fact, I'm sure YC didn't think watching people play games would be an important use. But there was something good in the idea. We already knew people love reality shows and like watching other people's lives. So the idea started from this: wouldn't it be cool if you could watch anyone's life? We believed in that idea, and it turned out games were the most successful part of it.

**QDaily: One step in YC's screening of applicants is a 10-minute interview. Do you ask the same questions every time?**

Altman: They're different every time.

The first question is always "What are you working on?"

The second is always "Why? Why this project?"

After that, the questions go in all directions. They're usually about the details of the project, such as "How do you plan to get users?", "How is your user growth so far?", "How do you plan to become a monopoly?" It could be anything.

**QDaily: You say intelligence and determination are a founder's most important qualities. What else?**

Altman: A very clear vision. A founder needs to know exactly what they are building and why.

It's very important to be able to explain clearly and precisely what your company is going to do.

**QDaily: Isn't that very rare? Facebook, for example, built a website for college students to look at each other's profiles, and Microsoft was just making software for a niche group at the time.**

Altman: A very small audience isn't really a problem, as long as they can define that audience precisely. What Facebook set out to do was always to connect you with your friends and let you see what they're doing. That's very clear. Microsoft was making software and operating systems for computers.

## What will YC do next? "Maybe we'll invest in a thousand companies a year"

**QDaily: What are your plans for the next year or two?**

Altman: We're going to get a lot bigger.

**QDaily: YC often says you either grow fast or die slowly. When YC talks about its own growth, how do you measure it?**

Altman: We look at total valuation.

For new companies, we look at their valuation in their first year at YC. It's not a perfect measure, because fundraising isn't the most important thing, but it does tell you something.

Even with companies like Airbnb that have been around for years and raised several rounds, we still work together a lot.

**QDaily: How do you help companies that have already raised Series A and Series B rounds? Will there be an incubation program for them?**

Altman: They still come by often to meet us and talk about how the company is going.

YC leans toward early-stage companies, but we stay in close contact with them at later stages too. We're considering a later-stage program like that, to give guidance to startups that have grown to a certain size.

It might happen next year.

**QDaily: If we look ahead to 2020, what kind of company will YC have become?**

Altman: Maybe we'll invest in a thousand companies a year, with programs covering startups at several different stages.

**QDaily: Will you invest more, too?**

Altman: Yes, we'll make more investments. But not Series A or Series B; we don't want to compete with venture capital firms. YC might invest in very late-stage companies, though.

That isn't settled yet. But we certainly can't do Series A investing, because that would put us in competition with venture capital firms. We can invest at a much later stage.

**QDaily: YC is doing more and more, and on a bigger and bigger scale. Do you think the meaning of "incubator" has changed over these years?**

Altman: I've never liked the name "incubator." Incubating isn't really what we do; the word sounds as if we're sitting on an egg waiting for it to hatch.

What we do is more about supporting startups and helping them move faster, so "accelerator" sounds more fitting. Some people also call us a "meta company," and I like that term better: YC is like a company made up of many smaller units, each of which is a startup. Lots of different companies together make one giant company.

## What has changed for Altman himself since he took over YC?

**QDaily: Before 2014, most people who didn't know YC especially well only knew Graham. Since he handed YC to you, has your personal life changed?**

Altman: I've become very, very popular. People stop me on the street and ask for photos.

**QDaily: Has your work changed much?**

Altman: Before, I spent all my time advising startups; now I spend half my time running the whole organization.

Every day different projects are under way, and I work with different partners. The other half goes to recruiting and selecting startups.

**QDaily: Graham once said you were like a young Bill Gates. But to young people today, Gates is more a rich, successful tycoon than the founder who took on IBM from nothing. When you hear the word "hacker," who is the first person who comes to mind?**

Altman: Elon Musk.

**QDaily: Not Zuckerberg?**

Altman: No. Elon's engineering achievements are extremely broad, and he is still deeply involved in the technical details today.

**QDaily: If you could go back 10 years, what advice would you give the young man building Loopt?**

Altman: "You can't build a product for a market that doesn't exist yet, a market that doesn't want to exist." Loopt's biggest problem was that people didn't want our product. That was before the iPhone; we were too early.

**QDaily: Do you miss being a founder?**

Altman: Yes, but actually my work at YC is a lot like running a startup. I spend most of my time running YC as a whole, not investing.

So this work still makes me feel like I'm running a startup. YC is a bit different from other investment firms, and I think that's a good thing.
